headline: Suki was originally the continuative stem of 透く (suku, “to leave a gap”).

sources.quote: Originally the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 透(す)く (suku, “to leave a gap”).

headline: Aji went from adi through adzi to azi, from Proto-Japonic *anti.

sources.quote: /adi/ → /ad͡ʑi/ → /aʑi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *anti.

headline: Shita is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sita.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sita.

headline: Ba, “place”, is an alteration of Old Japanese 庭 (nipa), modern 庭 (niwa, “garden, yard”).

sources.quote: /nipa/ → */niba/*/ⁿba/ → /ba/
An alteration from Old Japanese 庭 (nipa), modern 庭(にわ) (niwa, “garden, yard”).
First cited to a text from 1275.

headline: Gichō is 議 (“discussion”) plus 長 (“head”).

sources.quote: 議 (“discussion”) + 長 (“head”)

headline: Make is the continuative stem of 負ける (makeru, “to lose, to be defeated”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 負(ま)ける (makeru, “to lose, to be defeated”).

headline: Zonzuru is 存 (zon) plus する, with suru voiced to zuru.

sources.quote: 存(ぞん) (zon) + する (-suru, rendaku form する (zuru))

meaning: to exchange, to interchange, to substitute
headline: Kaeru, “to interchange”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the lower bigrade pattern.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 変(か)える (kaeru), 代(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

headline: Ōsama is 王 (ō) plus 様 (-sama).

sources.quote: 王(おう) (ō) + 様(さま) (-sama)

headline: Itami is a nominalization of 痛む (itamu, “to cause pain, hurt”).

sources.quote: Nominalization of 痛(いた)む (itamu, “to cause pain, hurt”).

headline: Iyagaru is 嫌 (iya, “despised”) plus がる (-garu, “to act like”).

sources.quote: Compound of 嫌 (iya, “despised”) + がる (-garu, “to act like”)

headline: Sei, “sex, gender”, is from Middle Chinese 性 (MC sjengH, “nature of something, inherent quality”), the kan'on, so a later borrowing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 性 (MC sjengH, “nature of something, inherent quality”).
The kan'on, so a later borrowing.

headline: Daimeishi is 代 (dai, “replacement”) plus 名詞 (meishi, “noun”), as it stands in for a noun.

sources.quote: From 代 (dai, “replacement”) + 名詞 (meishi, “noun”), as it stands in for a noun.

headline: Kawaigaru is 可愛い (kawaii, “cute, adorable”) plus がる (-garu, “feeling or thinking that way”).

sources.quote: Derived as compound of 可愛い (kawaii, “cute, adorable”) + がる (-garu, “feeling or thinking that way”, suffix applied to nouns and adjective stems to create a verb).

sources.quote: 筋 (“muscle; tendon”) + 肉 (“flesh”)

headline: Kūsō is Middle Chinese 空想, literally “fictional, fabricated + think, thought”; the fantasy sense is first cited in Japanese to 1886.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 空想 (khuwng sjang^X, literally “fictional, fabricated + think, thought”).
The sense of fantasy is first cited in Japanese to 1886, and probably reflects a Rangaku and Meiji era style of repurposing older terminology to translate unfamiliar Western concepts.

The Buddhist sense is older, and was borrowed into Japanese along with various Chinese Buddhist texts. This term is included in the 摩訶止観 (Maka Shikan), better known in English by its Chinese pronunciation, the Mohe Zhiguan, completed some time in the early 600s.

headline: Dakara is だ (“to be”) plus から (“because”).

sources.quote: だ (“to be”) + から (“because”)

meaning: to extend, to stretch, to reach out
headline: Nobasu, “to extend”, is cognate with 伸ばす (nobasu, “to grow, to spread”).

sources.quote: Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)ばす (nobasu, “to grow, to spread”).

headline: Heibon is Middle Chinese 平凡, literally “even, flat + in every case”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 平凡 (bjæng bjom, literally “even, flat + in every case”). Compare modern Min Nan reading pêng-hôan.

headline: Shinkū is first attested in the Kaifūsō anthology of 751, and its modern sense of vacuum in 1876.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 真空 (MC tsyin khuwng).
First attested in the 懐風藻 (Kaifūsō) anthology of Sinitic poetry written by Japanese authors, compiled in 751.
The modern sense of vacuum is first attested in 1876.

headline: Kumi is the continuative stem of 組む (kumu, “to assemble”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 組(く)む (kumu, “to assemble”).

headline: In chinō, 知 is a daiyōji replacing 智.

sources.quote: 知 is a daiyōji replacing 智.

headline: Obi is the continuative stem of 帯ぶ (obu, “to put something on the body”), first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

sources.quote: ⟨obi₁⟩ → */obʲi/ → /obi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ənpi.
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of 帯ぶ (obu, “to put something on the body”, transitive), following 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade conjugation”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

headline: Kōun is probably from Middle Chinese 幸運, literally “lucky fortune”.

sources.quote: /kauun/ → /kɔːun/ → /koːun/
Probably from Middle Chinese compound 幸運 /幸运 (hɛng^X hjunᴴ, literally “lucky fortune”).

headline: Sawagu shifted from older sawaku, a verbalization of さわ (sawa), the root of さわさわ (sawasawa, “noisily; rustling”).

sources.quote: Shift from older form さわく (sawaku), a verbalization of さわ (sawa), root of さわさわ (sawasawa, “noisily; rustling”).

headline: Koya is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 屋 (ya, “house, dwelling”).

sources.quote: 小(こ) (ko-, “little”) + 屋(や) (ya, “house, dwelling”)

headline: Mochi shifted from older mochii, historical mochihi; the page compares モモンガ (momonga) for a similar shift.

sources.quote: /mot͡ɕiː/ → /mot͡ɕi/
Shift from older mochii, historical mochihi (see below). Now the modern term for a glutinous rice cake.
Compare モモンガ (momonga, “Japanese dwarf flying squirrel”), with a similar shift.

headline: Seizei is a shift from 精誠 (seizei).

sources.quote: Shift from 精誠(せいぜい) (seizei).

sources.quote: Doublet of 勤(つと)める (tsutomeru).

headline: Rei, “gratitude; bow”, is from Middle Chinese 禮 (MC lejX).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 禮 (MC lejX).
